The guidelines provide a structured approach to developing a comprehensive multi-year plan (cMYP) for immunization, including both a planning tool and a costing tool. Managers are encouraged to review and assess the results of each step to ensure alignment with global targets, national policy priorities, and available resources. The cMYP is designed to be a dynamic document, periodically updated to adapt to changing conditions, generate empirically-based budget requests, and provide up-to-date information for advocacy and reporting. The cMYP guidelines represent one method for creating a multi-year plan. Many countries already have existing planning methods that address similar elements. In such cases, the cMYP guidelines and tools can serve as a reference to ensure quality and support national program planners. The main content areas of a multi-year immunization plan include: 1. Situation Analysis: This involves a review of health system barriers, successes, and promising practices, as well as identifying the strengths and weaknesses of the immunization system and disease control initiatives. 2. Objectives, Milestones, and Priority-Setting: This step outlines national goals, objectives, and strategies for three to five years, based on the situation analysis and priority-setting. 3. Activity Timeline and Monitoring and Evaluation Framework: This step establishes a timeline for key activities and milestones and develops a national monitoring and evaluation framework for all immunization components. 4. Costs, Financing, and Resource Mobilization: This includes costing and financing assessments linked to the relevant planning cycle and the Ministry of Health’s planning and budgeting cycles. It identifies financing gaps, resource mobilization strategies, and cost-benefit analyses. 5. Putting the cMYP into Action: This step involves creating detailed annual work plans and linking them to national planning and budgeting cycles at both national and sub-national levels. It also includes annual, midterm, and final reviews of the cMYP to adjust strategies based on lessons learned. The cMYP uses technical costing and planning tools to generate budget requests for priority social sector investments. While technical rigor is essential for planners and managers, the output must also be accessible to political leaders, ministries of finance, planning and education, non-state actors, the public, and even the media. A summary report should be published and disseminated in an accessible format, highlighting the main objectives, expected outcomes, and costs of the plan. The updated guidelines reflect significant developments in new vaccines, immunization technologies, and global health policies since their original development in 2005. These updates include: Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP): Ensures that strategies in the plan are comprehensive, using the GVAP as a framework. Links to Health Sector Planning: Emphasizes the integration of the national immunization program with health sector planning and financing, consolidating activities with other health interventions. Seven Planning Steps for Seven Immunization System Components: Aligns planning steps with health system building blocks and health sector strategies to support closer linkages between program and sector planning. Monitoring and Evaluation Frameworks: Develops a framework for tracking progress, including surveillance data, immunization expenditures, and inequalities. User-Friendly Costing and Financing Tools: Evaluates costs and financing to ensure financial sustainability with improved data entry and analysis tools. The GVAP, adopted by WHO Member States in 2012, aims to prevent millions of deaths by 2020 through equitable access to vaccines. It builds on the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy (GIVS) and emphasizes sustainable financing, country ownership, and innovation. Countries are expected to report progress annually through a common monitoring and evaluation framework. The GVAP outlines six strategic objectives: 1. All countries commit to immunization as a priority, supported by legal frameworks and independent technical advisory groups. 2. Individuals and communities understand the value of vaccines and demand immunization as their right and responsibility. 3. The benefits of immunization are equitably extended to all people, monitored through coverage gaps and equity indicators. 4. Strong immunization systems are integrated into well-functioning health systems, evaluated through dropout rates and data quality. 5. Immunization programs have sustainable access to predictable funding, quality supply, and innovative technologies. 6. Research and development innovations maximize the benefits of immunization, including advancements in vaccine efficacy and manufacturing capacity. The GVAP provides a roadmap for countries to innovate and address challenges, such as overburdened supply and logistics systems, increasing program delivery costs, and funding gaps. Achieving the Decade of Vaccines goals requires commitment from all stakeholders, regular monitoring, and alignment with national priorities and health sector goals.
